sources.entry: FreeSWITCH - Scalable open source cross-platform telephony platform. (Source Code) MPL-2.0 C

summary.one_liner: FreeSWITCH is an open source, cross-platform software telephony stack that turns commodity hardware into a SIP-capable telecom switch.
summary.what_it_does: The README describes FreeSWITCH as a Software Defined Telecom Stack meant to replace proprietary telecom switches with software that runs on commodity hardware, from a Raspberry Pi to a multi-core server. The source is available on GitHub and can be built for Linux, Windows, macOS and BSD. The README points to package-based installs (FSGET, Debian, Raspberry Pi, CentOS 7), source builds with Dockerfiles and dependency packages, Debian package building via FSDEB, and downloads for tarballs and Windows installers. It mentions mod_signalwire, a module distributed in the codebase for connecting to the SignalWire hosted cloud platform. Documentation, release notes, issue tracker and pull request workflow are linked from the README.
use_cases: run a self-hosted SIP or VoIP phone system
build a custom telephony or IVR application
interconnect calls with the outside world via SIP trunks
prototype telecom services on a Raspberry Pi
build telephony software from source on Linux or Windows
how_to_run: git clone the repository and checkout the development branch
Build from source following the Debian, Raspberry Pi or CentOS 7 tutorials linked in the README
Or install from packages using FSGET (recommended), or the Debian, Raspberry Pi or CentOS 7 tutorials
Or use the example Dockerfiles to build FreeSWITCH and its dependencies from source
Or download tarballs or the Windows installer from the Downloads section
notable: Software Defined Telecom Stack that runs from Raspberry Pi to multi-core servers
Cross-platform builds for Linux, Windows, macOS and BSD
Multiple install paths: packages (FSGET), source builds, Debian package builds, Docker examples
mod_signalwire module links the project to the SignalWire hosted cloud platform
Commercial support offered through the core team
caveats: Commercial support and hosted services come from SignalWire and professional services, which are separate from the open source project
The mailing list is archived, so the Slack community is the active channel
The README does not state detailed platform limits or hardware requirements
